transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Honestly, what made me come in is that I keep noticing I can’t stay seated during long sales strategy meetings. I know I’m supposed to just sit there and listen, but I’ll get up to refill my water, or I’ll kind of pace over by the printer for a minute. It’s not a huge dramatic thing, but it’s been happening enough that I’m starting to feel like I should talk to someone about it.
When you get up or pace during those meetings, is it because you feel anxious?

Not really anxious, no. It’s more like I just can’t stay in my seat for the whole meeting. I’ll get up for water or stand near the printer and pace a little, even though I know I’m supposed to be sitting and listening.
Does this urge to get up and move around also happen in other situations, like when you’re watching a movie or eating at a restaurant?

I mostly notice it in those long sales strategy meetings. That’s the main situation where I keep getting up even though I know I’m supposed to stay seated—like getting water or just pacing by the printer for a minute.
Outside of those meetings, do you often feel restless or fidgety?
I’m not really sure. I haven’t paid much attention to it outside of the meetings. I mean, I might shift around like anyone does, but I don’t know that I’d say it’s often.
As a child, did teachers or parents often say you had trouble staying seated?

Yeah, I think so. I remember it starting pretty early, like in elementary school, before high school. Teachers would write that I was bright, but I rushed through things, talked out of turn, forgot homework, and my desk was always stuffed with half-finished papers.
Do you currently have trouble focusing on what people are saying in meetings?

Yes, that does happen. Like if my manager is giving me feedback, or a client is explaining changes they want, I can be looking right at them and nodding, but then a few seconds later I realize I missed part of what they said and have to ask them to repeat it.
Do these attention lapses cause problems with getting your work done on time?

Yeah, sometimes. I’ll get most of a proposal or a CRM update done, but then I kind of leave off the last step—like I forget to send the final version or don’t log the follow-up—even though I meant to finish it. It doesn’t happen constantly, but it does create issues with timing.
Do these difficulties also cause problems for you at home?
I’m not really sure. I haven’t noticed a clear pattern at home the way I have at work. I mean, normal stuff gets busy, but I can’t think of a specific problem there right now.
At home, do these attention or restlessness problems ever cause you difficulties?
I’m not sure, honestly. I haven’t really noticed a clear issue at home from it. Maybe things get a little scattered sometimes, but I can’t point to a specific problem the way I can at work.
Do these attention or restlessness problems affect your driving?
I don’t think so. I haven’t noticed it affecting my driving in any clear way.
Have these attention or restlessness problems ever caused difficulties in your relationships?

I’m not sure. I can’t really think of a specific relationship problem that’s come from it. I mean, I might get distracted sometimes like anyone, but nothing that’s caused a clear issue with people close to me.
Do these problems ever make it hard for you to manage chores or errands at home?

Not so much chores or errands, but I do notice a similar thing with tasks. Like I’ll get most of a proposal or a CRM update done, and then somehow miss the last step—sending the final version or logging the follow-up—even though I fully meant to finish it.
Besides work, do you have these same attention problems in other settings?
I’m not really sure. I haven’t noticed the same kind of attention problems outside of work in a clear way. It’s mostly something I pick up on with work tasks.
Outside of work, do you also have trouble finishing tasks you intended to complete?

Not really outside of work, at least not that I can clearly point to. The main place I notice it is with work stuff—like I’ll get a proposal or CRM update almost done, and then I miss the final step, like sending it out or logging the follow-up, even though I meant to.
At home, do unfinished tasks ever create real problems for you?

At home, not really in a way that creates real problems. The clearest example for me is still work — I’ll get most of a proposal or CRM update done, and then I leave off the last step, like sending the final version or logging the follow-up, even though I meant to finish it.
Do you notice the same kinds of attention problems when you're doing hobbies or other activities outside of work?

I notice it more with things that feel kind of work-like, like longer strategy meetings or reading through a client brief. I’ll start out paying attention, but after a few minutes I realize I’ve just been staring at the same slide or paragraph and I don’t really know what the last point was. For actual hobbies outside of work, I don’t notice it as much.
Have these attention or restlessness problems ever caused trouble for you in school?

Yes. I mean, it goes back pretty far, even before high school. I remember in elementary school, teachers would say I was bright, but that I rushed through things or talked out of turn. I’d forget homework sometimes, and my desk was kind of a mess—stuffed with half-finished papers.
Have these attention or restlessness problems ever caused clear problems for you in social situations?

Yes, sometimes. Like if I’m in a meeting or someone’s walking through a deck, and I think of an idea, I’ll jump in or even pop over to add my thought. It’s not usually meant to be rude, but afterward I realize I probably interrupted or that it could have waited.

final_diagnosis.reason: The interview supports attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder with childhood onset and persistent symptoms into adulthood, including both inattentive features (missing spoken information, incomplete task follow-through, forgetting homework, half-finished work) and hyperactive/impulsive features (difficulty remaining seated, pacing, talking out of turn, interrupting). Symptoms were present before age 12 and have caused functional problems in school, work, and some social situations. Although cross-situational current symptoms were less clearly established outside work, the available candidate and transcript overall are most consistent with ADHD, unspecified type.
